posts.c: Star Wars became hugely popular because it combined an exciting adventure story with groundbreaking special effects. When George Lucas released the first film in 1977, audiences had rarely seen space battles, alien worlds, and futuristic technology portrayed so convincingly. Its memorable characters, including Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, and Princess Leia, helped make the story appealing to audiences of all ages. Another major reason was its enormous cultural influence. Star Wars introduced iconic lightsabers, unforgettable music by John Williams, and a fictional universe that fans could explore through toys, books, games, and sequels. Its simple story of good versus evil made it easy to connect with, while its detailed universe kept fans interested for decades. It transformed science fiction from a relatively niche genre into mainstream entertainment. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Hats were once an essential part of everyday fashion because they served both practical and social purposes. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, men and women wore hats to protect themselves from sunlight, rain, and cold weather. Hats also symbolized respectability, social status, and good manners. Going outside without one was sometimes considered improper, especially on formal occasions. Hat-wearing declined dramatically during the mid-20th century as fashion became more casual, cars became widespread, and elaborate hairstyles grew popular. President John F. Kennedy is sometimes blamed for ending the hat trend, although it was already declining before his presidency. Interestingly, there was a time when leaving home without a hat could seem almost as unusual as leaving without shoes today. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: Pirates were far more organized than movies suggest, especially during the Golden Age of Piracy between the 1650s and 1730s. Many pirate crews elected their captains, voted on important decisions, and followed written rules. Some even had compensation systems for injured crew members. Interestingly, pirates rarely buried treasure, and the famous practice of making prisoners walk the plank was much less common than Hollywood suggests. Another surprising fact is that pirates sometimes used intimidation to avoid fighting altogether. The famous skull-and-crossbones flag, known as the Jolly Roger, warned ships to surrender before an attack. Pirates also included women, such as Anne Bonny and Mary Read, who became notorious in the early 18th century. Despite their reputation for lawlessness, some pirate crews operated with surprisingly democratic rules, at least among their own members. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: A big yawn mid-stretch makes for a deceptive image. Most of us are aware that wolves do not impersonate grannies to trick children or huff and puff houses to the ground. Still, the archetype of the “big bad wolf” persists in folklore and fiction. Fairy tales like Little Red Riding Hood seem harmless enough, but as biodiversity plummets across the world, suddenly the fictitious villain becomes a very real and very convenient scapegoat. When local wildlife begins to decline, predators are often unfairly blamed for the loss, despite the fact that habitat destruction and development play a much larger role. My hope in sharing the beauty of animals like wolves in my new book Reverence is to inspire empathy and encourage us to reevaluate how we coexist with our planet’s predators. posts.c: Product reviews have a powerful influence on what people buy, with many shoppers trusting feedback from strangers almost as much as personal recommendations. Interestingly, products with a few negative reviews can sometimes appear more trustworthy than those with nothing but perfect ratings, because a flawless review history may seem suspicious. Another surprising fact is that people are more likely to leave reviews after extremely good or bad experiences than after ordinary ones. This can make online ratings less representative of the average customer’s experience. Fake reviews also complicate matters, which is why a detailed, balanced three-star review can sometimes tell you more than dozens of enthusiastic five-star ratings. Like this content? posts.c: What makes a good café? The criteria depend on the coffee drinker. Maybe you’re a purist who’s obsessed with direct sourcing of single-origin beans. Maybe you’re a nerd, in which case you’re all about the latest laboratory-like brewing method. Or maybe you prefer a place that serves up sweet and seasonal drinks, with comfy couches upon which to plop and enjoy them. The latest batch of cafés to open around Chittenden County isn’t fussy. None of them has a pour-over on the menu or a siphon behind the bar. But they all make a good cup of coffee — or tea, if that’s your thing. And alongside the lattes and local pastries, they serve a big dose of charm, from interactive art to stacks of books. We headed to five spots that opened this year to sip seasonal lattes, dirty sodas, classic espresso drinks and cold-foam chai. At each, we found a bonus element — something beyond the beverages — that helps bring people in. Find the full story wherever you get Seven Days or at the link in bio! ☕️ 🥐 ✍️

posts.c: Since the founding of the city, Parisians had been burying their dead in the middle of town, which led to an untenable situation: In the spring of 1780, heavy rains wrecked a burial mound at the overcrowded Les Innocents cemetery, sending a wave of decaying corpses tumbling into the building next door. The king’s solution to necrotic overpopulation? Shut down all of Paris’s graveyards and transfer all the bodies to an extensive network of underground tunnels left behind by 13th-century limestone miners—a task that took 12 years to complete. Today, morbid-minded tourists—like our @cntraveler editorial operations manager, @tayloreisenhauer, who captured these photos—can visit @catacombesdeparis_officiel. There, you can explore about a mile of this underground labyrinth’s 200 miles of bone-lined walls, greeted by this friendly inscription: "Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la mort" (Stop! This is the empire of death).

posts.c: Someone tell Belle I found her library in Vermont. 📚♥️ The @stjohnsburyathenaeum is straight out of Beauty and the Beast, with ornate woodwork and spiral staircases inside a building that’s been welcoming readers for more than 150 years. It’s such an unusual find in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, right on Main Street, and the library is only part of the reason to visit. Horace Fairbanks gave the Athenaeum to the community in 1871, and it opened with 8,000 books. I love that it still serves as the town’s public library. Imagine getting to call this your neighborhood reading spot, with sunlight coming through those tall, arched windows while you settle into a book. Then there’s the art gallery, added in 1873, where paintings in heavy gilded frames hang one above another in a setting that preserves the feel of a 19th-century museum. After dropping my children at school, I headed straight there with my camera, hoping the overnight frost would transform the tiny slime moulds into something special. The iridescent fruiting bodies surrounded by intricate ice crystals created a magical, almost otherworldly scene. With the frost disappearing quickly, I had only a limited time to capture this extraordinary moment in nature. This photograph reminds me that some of the most beautiful discoveries can be found in the most unexpected places, sometimes just around the corner from home." - Kutub Uddin (@kutub_uddin_macro_man) This week's #WPY62 guest is Kutub Uddin, winner of #WPY62's Portfolio Award. posts.c: Our Sun knows how to get in the spirit! 🎃 Years ago, our Solar Dynamics Observatory caught our Sun looking like a jack-o’-lantern, with active regions shaped like a carved face. Swipe to see other cosmic curiosities captured over the years. #NASA #Halloween #Space The wispy white gas of this star-forming cloud, Lupus 3, is 500 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. It looks something like a wave of ectoplasm or stretch of cobwebs. Which do you see? As we set our sights on the Hourglass Nebula, it appears to gaze back at us. This creepy cosmic object is a planetary nebula, the glowing relic of a dying, Sun-like star. This ghoulish cloud of gas and dust, called the Ghost Nebula, is 550 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia. Its long ghostly veil is shaped by radiation from the bright stars embedded within it. This witch is busy brewing baby stars! Named the Witch Head, this nebula is found 800 light-years away in the constellation Orion, just off the hunter’s “knee.”

posts.c: New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. posts.c: Creating my book Reverence required endless hours of slogging through over 2 million images in my digital archives. In my bleary-eyed scrolling haze, I suddenly came across images I hadn’t seen in years. The polar bear above visited my cabin in the middle of a blizzard in Svalbard, and you can see in the series how she first peeked in before pawing at the window. The third image, titled Face to Face, became one of my best known prints and is the only image of mine I have ever felt compelled to hang my home. posts.c: This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. posts.c: You're in for a spooky trip that goes beyond your average ghost tour in New Orleans, Louisiana, known for its spiritual history, centuries-old cemeteries, French Quarter legends, and NOLA Halloween spirit, captured here by @nocturnalnola. Commerce writer @jeschapel knows the best way to do it, starting with the city's roots in voodoo: a spiritual tradition shaped by West African practices, Catholicism, and the Haitian diaspora. You can dig into the history of Marie Laveau—the legendary 19th-century voodoo practitioner whose name still pops up all over the city—at @mlhouseofvoodoo in the French Quarter. Or you can take an expert-led voodoo tour, where you'll learn all about the history and how it's ingrained in the city's culture today. @voodoomuseum can also help put the traditions into context. Be sure to also make your way to the Garden District to visit Buckner Mansion, the enormous Greek Revival house built in 1857 that American Horror Story: Coven fans will recognize as Miss Robic

posts.c: A multi-million-dollar effort to improve water quality at Vermont’s only “lake in crisis” appears to have been successful, according to scientists at the Department of Environmental Conservation. Lake Carmi has been plagued for years by pervasive cyanobacteria blooms that close beaches and prevent people from going in the water. State officials named Carmi a “lake in crisis” in 2018, prioritizing it for funding and cleanup. In internal emails, DEC staff said the blooms generated an "extremely thick sludge" that routinely built up at the North end of the lake in the summer. Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photos by dopaminergic/Flickr, courtesy of Seth Anderson and Mike Tansey.

posts.c: Decay is in the air this season, made manifest in “(Un)Becoming,” a show of works by Ana Koehler (@ana_koehler) and Hannah Cieri (@cierifab) at Soapbox Arts (@soapboxartsvt) in Burlington. Koehler presents collaged, figurative paintings on panel of women in violent but symbiotic-seeming relationships with the garden: one pricked by thorns, another ripping tulips from the ground, a third feeding crows with her own blood, in the style of an old-school saint. The artist complements these with photographic images of plants, hair and body parts pressed directly onto a scanner bed, with accents sewn on in gold thread. posts.c: A tiny woodland discovery 🌲 "Found in Bognor Regis, West Sussex, just a 10-minute walk from my home, this delicate little fungus was growing on a blackberry thorn. Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. posts.c: What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Have you ever visited a museum that feels like everything might come to life after the doors close? 👀 Tucked away in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, the Fairbanks Museum & Planetarium in St. Johnsbury feels like stepping straight into Night at the Museum. And with Halloween around the corner, I can’t think of a more fitting place to explore! 🎃 Founded in 1889 by local industrialist Franklin Fairbanks, this extraordinary Victorian museum began as a collection of natural wonders and artifacts gathered from around the world. posts.c: In 2015, Alejandro Bergad and Jacob Goldstein cofounded what would become Sunsoil, a Hardwick company that grows, processes and sells organic, hemp-derived products. The new company burned down an old shed on its property to make room for a new, large barn for drying hemp — and within a few years had become a major manufacturer of cannabidiol, or CBD, wellness supplements. Its certified-organic products are sold in 2,500 stores nationwide and through direct-to-consumer marketing. But Sunsoil could soon see its business razed, as it and other CBD companies face the biggest threat to their livelihood since Congress legalized hemp production in 2018. A new federal law, scheduled to take effect on December 11, closes a legal loophole that inadvertently allowed hemp companies to sell products that contain intoxicating tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, with few, if any, restrictions or oversight. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Here's something to warm your heart on a chilly fall day! These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

posts.c: Sonar with a side of squeaks! Bats have a remarkable ability called echolocation, which allows them to navigate in the dark by making high-pitched sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. Essentially, they shout into the void and wait for the void to explain where everything is. Same. Still waiting… These sound waves help bats locate insects, avoid obstacles, and navigate their surroundings with impressive accuracy. They can even detect objects as small as human hair. Meanwhile, some humans have been known to walk into a glass door in broad daylight. One time. Moving on. Bats are an important part of many national park ecosystems, helping control insect populations and keeping nature ticking along after dark. So, the next time you hear a bat making noises, remember it isn’t screaming into the darkness. Well, it is, but it’s using a highly sophisticated biological sonar system. Screaming with purpose. Try it. Watch out for that door. NPS Photos: Bats flying in the darkness

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: The spirit bears of my new book Reverence. Over ten years ago, a @natgeo assignment sent me deep into the Great Bear Rainforest in search of the elusive spirit bear. At the time, big oil interests were pushing a pipeline from Canada’s Tar Sands to British Columbia, threatening the waterways that sustain the rainforest. First Nations communities were leading the fight against the project, and the magazine was after images that could rally the public behind them. Which is how I found myself crouched at the mossy edge of a cold stream, mesmerized as, just inches away, a spirit bear fished from the rushing waters. Under the guidance of @gitgaatspirit, I spent weeks in that mossy kingdom getting to know the wise little spirits that call it home. Soon after the story was finally published, the pipeline project was defeated. Reverence is now available in a limited print run, of which only a few thousand copies remain. posts.c: Oh, so THAT’S what an “ongoing” work means…. Swing by “Catalyst: Art as Inquiry” before it closes on December 12, 2026. And even if you’d seen, Heimo Wallner’s “Last Note (Echo),” 2026 before, you’re going to want to take another look. From the artist: I draw, and this ongoing process manifests itself in piles of drawings, animations and when possible: room drawings—made quickly, with a clear deadline, these wall drawings force me to generate imagery on the spot and little strands of narratives crystallize, interweave, connect, and disrupt. They become rhythm, texture, ornament: wallpaper. The human condition is my quarry. Stupidity (my own and the general)—an endless source. The banal and the essential, daily news vs eternal truths, private painful secrets turn into practical jokes—catharsis and damnation all at once.

posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: (News Release) Most Yellowstone National Park roads and entrances will close to regular vehicle traffic on Nov. 1 in preparation for winter. Each year, the park closes its West, South and East entrances, along with nearly all roads, to prepare for winter operations and the start of snowmobile and snowcoach travel season on Dec. 15. As a result, Saturday, Oct. 31 will be the final day visitors can drive most of Yellowstone’s roads in 2026. The road from Tower Fall to Canyon Junction (Dunraven Pass) will remain open through Oct. 31, weather permitting. Visitors traveling to Yellowstone by car during the winter can access the park only via the road connecting the North Entrance in Gardiner, Montana, and the Northeast Entrance in Cooke City/Silver Gate, Montana. This route passes through Mammoth Hot Springs, Tower Junction and Lamar Valley and remains open year-round, weather permitting. posts.c: Ever look at all the rain hitting your roof and wonder how much water you’re letting go to waste? A rainwater capture system puts that water to work. Every inch of rain falling on a 1,000-square-foot roof can produce around 600 gallons of water. Gutters collect the runoff and direct it into a system that can help keep your garden watered. The science is all about collecting and filtering water before it reaches storage. A leaf filter catches larger debris, while a first flush diverter sends the dirtiest initial runoff away from the tank. This matters because dust, bird droppings, and other contaminants can build up on your roof between rainfalls. Removing that initial runoff helps keep your stored water cleaner. This rainwater capture system stores up to 5,750 gallons across the property, with underground pipes directing collected water into a main 5,000-gallon tank. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! posts.c: Formerly Sugarsnap Farm, Wet Foot Farm is now owned and operated by Patrick Shafer, Jamie Cohen, and Abbey Duke. They’re one of seven farm operations growing food on land leased from the Intervale Center! Alongside produce for Sugarsnap Catering, the farm grows pawpaws—North America’s largest native edible fruit. With a creamy texture and hints of mango and banana, pawpaws naturally grow in moist forests and along waterways. Adapted to periodic flooding, these perennial trees support healthy ecosystems by stabilizing soil, reducing erosion, and providing wildlife habitat. Their resilience makes them a promising crop for climate-resilient agriculture. Pawpaw trees take several years to produce fruit, making growing them a long-term investment. Abbey Duke planted the original pawpaw trees in 2010 and in 2021, Patrick and Jamie began cultivating and planting more trees to meet growing demand, and they plan to continue expanding production in the coming years. posts.c: So @jacquesinthegarden stumbled across a mystery pomegranate tree growing near his house, and the fruit turned out to be the sweetest he’d ever tasted. The science comes down to genetics. Pomegranates grown from seed can have a unique combination of genes from their parent plants, so the fruit may taste completely different from what you’d expect. That’s why this mystery tree outperformed one he had intentionally grown for three years. If you find a pomegranate with incredible flavor, you’ll want to clone it rather than grow it from seed. Hardwood cuttings can develop roots and grow into genetically identical plants, preserving the traits that made the original fruit so good. Keeping those cuttings warm while providing indirect light can help encourage root development, especially during cooler weather. And here’s the fun part: birds like crows can spread seeds to new places, creating unexpected seedlings throughout a neighborhood. You might not know what you’re growing until it fruits

posts.c: Our Intervale Conservation Nursery grows thousands of native trees and shrubs each year, but our work doesn’t stop there! 🌱 This year, our Nursery Crew is also caring for 50 acres of young forests across Vermont. At Riverside Park in Warren, we’re working with the Town of Waitsfield and Friends of the Mad River to restore 2 acres along the Mad River. Along with removing invasive knotweed around young trees, we’re building living barriers from willow branches that take root and sprout! These natural barriers will help stabilize riverbanks, prevent invasive knotweed from spreading, and protect water quality throughout the Lake Champlain Basin. Healthy rivers and soils are the foundation of healthy farms and food systems! This critical stewardship work to restore riparian forest buffers is possible thanks to funding from the Lake Champlain Basin Program and Great Lakes Fishery Commission. posts.c: THE hottest color of the season is hunter orange! Not only does fluorescent orange make a chic fashion statement, but more importantly, it keeps hunters and all outdoor recreators visible to other people in the woods. Wearing a hunter orange hat or vest is important for everyone in the woods during hunting season. Whether you're hunting, bird watching, or trail running, bright orange can help you be seen, even in low-light. While it isn’t recommended to wear orange during waterfowl and turkey seasons, we do still suggest folks chasing fall ducks, geese and turkey wear hunter orange when going to and from blind tree stands or calling spots. Same goes for bowhunters walking up to their treestands or climbing down at the end of the day. Be smart and safe outdoors this fall. Wear orange!

posts.c: We created a fleet of no-cost, seriously spooky, DIY witches brooms, with cuttings from our own yard.⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ Start by cutting small bundles of ornamental grass and hang them upside down to dry (you can skip the drying part). Cut branches to size (we got ours from our birch tree) and on one end wrap and knot twine - making sure to leave a 6” tail. Then, center the branch in a grass bundle before wrapping the grass with twine to keep it in place. Use the tail to tie off. Trim the grass to your desired length. Last, use a hook or just tie string around the other end of the branch to hang. ⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ We love the look and it was the perfect project to get us started on a very spooky exterior 🧙‍♀️⠀⠀ •⠀⠀ #renovationhusbands #diy #diydecor #halloween #halloweendecor diyhalloween

posts.c: Checking in on my Peace Lily - one of my first plants! - Light analysis: in a white LED grow light context, you need to specify the strength (FC or µmol/s/m² is fine) and the duration - you can calculate the DLI by multiplying the strength and the duration (along with the appropriate conversions) - For this plant: 90 FC x 14 hours gives you a DLI of 0.8 mol/day, which is quite low but clearly still enough to produce some flowers. With a higher DLI, my plant would have probably produced more flowers but I'm happy with where this plant is and how it has grown for now - The spent leaves on a peace lily don't tend to fall off on their own like a pothos or philodendron so you should regularly cut them off once they're fully dead - staying on top of it will allow space for new leaves to grow (mine has become a bit crowded!) - #houseplantjournal #peacelily #spathyphyllum

Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,
